description.text: Teresa of Avila, born Teresa Sánchez de Cepeda Dávila y Ahumada on 28 March 1515, entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation at the age of twenty and soon became a leading mystic of the Counter‑Reformation.  Her early years were marked by intense asceticism and a series of ecstatic visions, the most famous of which was the transverberation in which a golden lance pierced her heart, a moment that later inspired Gianlorenzo Bernini’s celebrated sculpture.

In the following decades Teresa transformed the Carmelite order, founding the Discalced Carmelites with the help of John of the Cross and establishing a strict rule of poverty and prayer.  Her writings—most notably *The Interior Castle* and *The Way of Perfection*—became foundational texts for Christian mysticism.  She was canonised in 1622 by Pope Gregory XV and, in 1970, became the first woman to be named a Doctor of the Church by Pope Paul VI.

curiosities.text: Teresa’s vision of a golden lance piercing her heart inspired Gianlorenzo Bernini’s famous sculpture *The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa* in Rome.
She was canonised by Pope Gregory XV in 1622, forty years after her death.
In 1970 Pope Paul VI declared Teresa the first female Doctor of the Church, a title she shares with Catherine of Siena.
Her book *The Interior Castle* uses the metaphor of a seven‑mansion castle to describe the stages of spiritual growth.
Teresa founded the Discalced Carmelites, a reformed branch of the Carmelite order that emphasized poverty, silence and contemplative prayer.
